item.title: Arima Onsen: Japan's Oldest Hot Spring, Behind Kobe — Guide
item.description: Arima Onsen lies in a wooded valley behind Mount Rokko, barely half an hour from central Kobe yet feeling like a mountain village. It is one of Japan’s three most ancient hot springs, mentioned in eighth-century chronicles and patronised by emperors and by the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and it is famous for two entirely different waters rising side by side: kinsen, the ‘gold water’, heavily iron-rich and salty, which oxidises to a rust-brown on contact with air, and ginsen, the clear ‘silver water’ carrying carbonate and radium.

item.title: Maiko Park: Under the Bridge, Over the Strait — Guide
item.description: Maiko Park occupies the narrow strip of Kobe shoreline directly beneath the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge, and it exists to let you get close to the thing. Its centrepiece is the Maiko Marine Promenade, a walkway built into the bridge structure that carries you 150 metres out over the water on a deck 47 metres up, with glass floor panels looking straight down at the churning tidal currents. In the same grounds stands the Ijokaku, a striking octagonal green villa built in 1915 for a Chinese merchant, along with pines, sea views and picnic lawns.

item.title: Nankinmachi: Kobe's Chinatown — Guide
item.description: Nankinmachi, Kobe’s Chinatown, is one of only three in Japan and grew from the Chinese merchant community that settled here after the port opened to foreign trade in 1868. Compact and lively, it centres on a small square with an ornate pavilion, entered through vivid red-and-gold gates and lined with lanterns overhead. The real draw is the street food: stalls and shopfronts sell steaming buta-man pork buns, dumplings, fried noodles, sweet sesame balls and roast duck, and the pleasure is simply to graze your way through the lanes with something hot in each hand.

item.title: Oji Zoo: Kobe's Family Zoo Under the Cherry Trees — Guide
item.description: Oji Zoo is Kobe’s much-loved city zoo, a compact and refreshingly inexpensive place set in parkland between Nada and Sannomiya. Its collection covers the usual favourites — elephants, big cats, giraffes and a well-known group of koalas — alongside a small old-fashioned amusement corner with rides for younger children and a preserved Meiji-era Western residence in the grounds. In spring the zoo’s cherry trees make it one of the best hanami spots in central Kobe, when families picnic under the blossoms between animal enclosures.

item.title: Sorakuen Garden: Kobe's Finest Traditional Garden — Guide
item.description: Sorakuen is the finest traditional Japanese garden in Kobe, laid out in the Meiji era as the private grounds of a former city mayor and opened to the public after the war. Its winding paths circle a pond fed by a waterfall, passing through groves of pine, camphor and maple in the middle of the modern city. Two unusual buildings share the grounds: the Hassam House, a Western-style villa built for a British trader in Kobe’s foreign settlement, and a rare surviving feudal-lord’s stable relocated here — and each May the garden’s several thousand azaleas turn it brilliant.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Hyogo: From Arima Onsen Suites to Kobe Harbor Views
item.description: Hyogo Prefecture presents an accommodation landscape unlike any other in Japan. Within a single prefecture you can sleep in one of the country’s oldest and most storied onsen towns, bathe in a natural spring that runs a distinctive rust-red colour, wake to views of a harbor where the lights of a cosmopolitan port city still shimmer, or step out of your ryokan onto the main street of a historic onsen town in a yukata to visit seven different public bathhouses on a single evening.

item.title: Hyogo Haunted Spots: Ghost Legends of Himeji Castle & Eerie Battlefields
item.description: Hyogo Prefecture carries more accumulated history than almost any other region in Japan — centuries of castle politics and clan conflict, a cataclysmic earthquake that reshaped a modern city overnight, medieval sea battles that ended dynasties and drowned emperors. This history has left its mark not only in museums and ruins but in legend, atmosphere, and the particular quality of certain places after dark. The ghost stories that have grown up around Hyogo’s most resonant sites are not invented entertainment; they are the cultural memory of real events that Japanese people have found too heavy to hold in plain historical language alone.

item.title: Hyogo Honeymoon: Romantic Onsen Ryokan & Kobe Night Views
item.description: Japan’s most romantic prefecture is not Kyoto, despite what every brochure suggests. Hyogo Prefecture — with its mountain hot springs rising above ancient cedar forests, its harbor city lit like a constellation after dark, its willow-lined canal towns where couples float between seven bathhouses in silk robes — offers a honeymoon architecture that Kyoto’s tourist density has long made impossible to sustain. The scale is right. The luxury is present without ostentatious display.

item.title: Hyogo Leisure: Jazz Bars, Sake Breweries & Harbor Cruises
item.description: Kobe has always been a city that knows how to enjoy itself. Its history as Japan’s most cosmopolitan port city — open to foreign trade from 1868, home to settled European and Chinese merchant communities within a generation — left a cultural legacy that distinguishes it from every other Japanese city. The architecture is different, the food culture is different, the music is different, and the pace of an evening out carries a particular ease that visitors from Tokyo and Osaka both notice immediately.

item.title: Hyogo Solo Travel Guide
item.description: Japan is the world’s most comfortable country for solo travel, and Hyogo Prefecture is one of its finest arguments. A prefectural geography that spans a world-heritage castle, Japan’s oldest hot spring, a cosmopolitan harbor city, a sake-producing coastal district, and an onsen canal town means that a solo traveler can spend a week moving between fundamentally different experiences without once feeling that a companion was required to make any of them work.

item.title: Hyogo Top Sightseeing: Himeji Castle, Kobe Harborland & Beyond
item.description: Hyogo Prefecture stretches across an astonishing range of landscapes and histories, from the gleaming white ramparts of Japan’s most celebrated castle to the cosmopolitan harbor districts of Kobe, from sacred mountain temples hidden in cedar forest to the crashing tidal maelstroms of the Seto Inland Sea. Few Japanese prefectures pack such genuine variety into a single itinerary, and fewer still can claim a World Heritage Site, a 19th-century foreign quarter, and a record-breaking suspension bridge all within an hour of each other.
